title: Satisficing vs Maximizing: when to decide fast and when to obsess
summary: Jason Cohen separates maximizing (finding the best option) from satisficing (taking the first acceptable one) and argues you must pick deliberately for each decision. Speed is a startup's edge, so satisfice almost everything, and save maximizing for slow, foundational calls like product and business strategy.

principles.text: Decide on purpose whether each decision calls for maximizing or satisficing.
principles.quote: You must choose when to Maximize, and when to Satisfice.

principles.text: Speed is a major competitive advantage, and it requires satisficing rather than maximizing.
principles.quote: Speed is one of the greatest competitive advantages, partially explaining why small up-starts are able to beat large incumbents. Speed requires satisficing, not maximizing.

principles.text: Ship and let customer reaction and real data pick your next move instead of planning many moves ahead.
principles.quote: using customer reaction and real data to decide your next move, rather than planning many moves ahead

principles.text: Maximize product and business strategy, since teams and careers are built on it and it shouldn't change often.
principles.quote: Strategy isn't something you want to change often, with entire teams and careers being built on top of it, so maximization is best.

principles.text: Perfectionists tend to over-maximize, so default to satisficing for anything that isn't a major decision.
principles.quote: Be careful; the same perfectionism that makes you a force to be reckoned with (and that drives your impostor syndrome) will lead you to maximize too often.

principles.text: For areas you satisfice, set an objective bar for 'good enough' and stop investing once you clear it.
principles.quote: For satisfying activities, define an objective threshold for "what is satisfactory."
